questions.title: Does DPO assume there are only two possible responses for each prompt?
questions.question_body: I may be misunderstanding the setup of Direct Preference Optimization. The training data always seems to be a prompt $x$ together with a preferred answer $y_w$ and a dispreferred answer $y_l$. That makes it look like the model is only learning to choose between two fixed responses, but language modeling has an enormous output space. How does optimizing on pairwise comparisons over $(y_w, y_l)$ translate into a policy over all possible completions $y$ for the same prompt?

questions.title: Why does the Bradley-Terry preference model depend only on the difference $r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2)$?
questions.question_body: In the paper, human preferences are modeled as $p^*(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x)=\sigma(r^*(x,y_1)-r^*(x,y_2))$. I understand this algebraically, but I do not understand the modeling assumption. Why should preference probabilities depend only on the reward difference and not on the absolute reward values? Is this just a convenient parameterization, or is there a deeper reason that makes this the right choice for preference data?

questions.title: How do you derive $\pi_r(y\mid x) \propto \pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)$ from the KL-constrained RLHF objective?
questions.question_body:
The paper says that for the objective
$$
\max_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{y\sim \pi(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)] - \beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(y\mid x)\|\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)),
$$
the optimal policy has the closed form
$$
\pi_r(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\right).
$$
I can see that this looks like a Gibbs distribution, but I am not following the derivation. Is this obtained with a Lagrange multiplier enforcing $\sum_y \pi(y\mid x)=1$? If so, can someone show the steps carefully?

questions.title: Why does the partition function $Z(x)$ cancel out when DPO rewrites the Bradley-Terry model in terms of policies?
questions.question_body:
The key step in the paper seems to be rewriting the reward as
$$
r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x),
$$
and then substituting this into the Bradley-Terry probability for comparing two responses. The paper says the $\beta \log Z(x)$ term cancels because the Bradley-Terry model only uses reward differences. I understand that both responses share the same prompt $x$, but I still feel like I am missing something subtle. Could someone write out the substitution explicitly and explain why there is no hidden dependence on $y$ left in $Z(x)$?

questions.title: If the original RLHF objective is an expectation over $y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)$, why does DPO not need on-policy sampling during training?
questions.question_body: In standard RLHF, the optimization objective involves sampling responses from the current policy because we are maximizing expected reward under $\pi_\theta$. But DPO trains on a fixed offline dataset of preference pairs and uses a binary cross-entropy loss instead. If DPO is supposedly optimizing the same KL-regularized objective, why is it valid to remove the on-policy sampling step entirely? Is the equivalence exact, or only exact under the Bradley-Terry model and infinite data?

questions.title: How is $\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ computed for a full response in DPO?
questions.question_body:
The DPO loss uses terms like $\log \pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)$ and $\log \pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)$, where $y$ is a whole text completion rather than a single token. For an autoregressive language model, is this just the sum of token log-probabilities,
$$
\log \pi_\theta(y\mid x)=\sum_t \log \pi_\theta(y_t\mid x, y_{<t})?
$$
If so, does DPO implicitly prefer shorter responses because they involve fewer terms, or is length handled in some special way?

questions.title: What exactly does the hyperparameter $\beta$ control in DPO?
questions.question_body:
The paper says $\beta$ controls how far the policy can deviate from the reference model, but I am confused about the direction of the effect. In the optimal policy formula,
$$
\pi_r(y\mid x) \propto \pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta),
$$
smaller $\beta$ seems to magnify reward differences, which would make the policy less conservative. In the DPO loss, however, $\beta$ multiplies the log-ratio terms. Can someone give an intuitive explanation of how changing $\beta$ changes the learned policy, and why this is consistent with the KL-regularization view?

questions.title: Why is the implicit reward in DPO defined as $\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)}$ instead of just using $\log \pi_\theta(y\mid x)$?
questions.question_body:
The paper says 'your language model is secretly a reward model' and then defines an implicit reward
$$
\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)}.
$$
I do not understand why the reward is a log-ratio against the reference policy rather than simply the model's own log-probability of the response. Is the point that reward should measure how much the trained policy departs from the reference? How should I interpret this quantity conceptually?

questions.title: How is DPO different from unlikelihood training if both increase $\log \pi(y_w\mid x)$ and decrease $\log \pi(y_l\mid x)$?
questions.question_body:
The paper compares DPO to unlikelihood-style training and says the important difference is a weight of the form
$$
\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)).
$$
But at a high level both methods seem to do the same thing: make the preferred answer more likely and the dispreferred answer less likely. Can someone explain, maybe with a simple example, what this weighting changes in practice and why removing it can lead to degeneration?

questions.title: What does the gradient weight $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$ mean intuitively?
questions.question_body:
The DPO gradient is written as a preference update multiplied by
$$
\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)).
$$
The paper says this gives higher weight when the implicit reward model ranks the dispreferred answer too highly. I am trying to build intuition for the extremes. If the model already strongly prefers $y_w$, does this term go near $0$ and almost stop learning on that pair? If the model strongly prefers $y_l$, does it go near $1$ and apply a large correction? Is this basically a margin-based hard-example weighting?

questions.title: What prevents DPO from collapsing to extreme probabilities on the training pairs?
questions.question_body:
Since the DPO loss rewards making the preferred completion more likely than the dispreferred one, I would expect the model to drive
$$
\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_w\mid x)} - \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_l\mid x)}
$$
to be as large as possible on every training example. Why does this not just push the model toward memorizing the dataset or making probabilities overly sharp? Is the only protection the reference model in the ratio, or is there some other regularizing effect in the DPO objective?

questions.title: Why are reward functions that differ by a prompt-only term $f(x)$ considered equivalent?
questions.question_body:
In the theoretical section, the paper defines two reward functions as equivalent if
$$
r(x,y)-r'(x,y)=f(x)
$$
for some function depending only on the prompt. I can see that this would cancel in pairwise reward differences, but the paper also claims that such reward functions induce the same optimal policy under the KL-constrained RL objective. Could someone explain both claims carefully? I want to understand why adding a prompt-dependent constant changes neither the preference probabilities nor the optimal policy.

questions.title: How should I interpret the theorem that any Bradley-Terry-consistent reward class can be written as $r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)}$?
questions.question_body:
The main theorem says that, under mild assumptions, all reward classes consistent with the Plackett-Luce or Bradley-Terry preference model can be represented through the reparameterization
$$
r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)}.
$$
This sounds very strong, and I am not sure what is being claimed. Is the theorem saying that DPO loses no expressive power compared with an explicit reward model, except for the usual ambiguity of adding $f(x)$? Also, what are the 'mild assumptions' doing here, and are there realistic cases where they fail?

questions.title: What happens in DPO if the preference dataset was generated from a different reference policy than the one used for training?
questions.question_body:
The paper mentions that in practice preference datasets may come from some unavailable SFT model, and if that model is not available they fit a new $\pi_\text{ref}$ by maximum likelihood on the preferred completions. I am confused about why this is reasonable. Since the derivation uses the actual reference policy inside
$$
\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)},
$$
wouldn't using the wrong $\pi_\text{ref}$ change the implied reward and therefore the whole objective? Is this only an approximation to reduce distribution shift?

questions.title: If DPO and PPO optimize the same KL-regularized reward objective, why can DPO outperform PPO in the experiments?
questions.question_body: One of the most surprising claims in the paper is that DPO and PPO target the same underlying RLHF objective, yet DPO often gets a better reward-KL frontier and even beats PPO with access to ground-truth rewards. If the optimization target is the same, should they not converge to the same solution given enough capacity? Is the difference purely due to PPO optimization instability and variance, or does DPO actually optimize a different practical objective once function approximation and finite data are taken into account?
